1.	Has the government received a report with respect to the wreck of the SS. Trader in March, on the rocks dumped off the end of the jetty on the north arm of the Fraser river, British Columbia, built by the government ?
2.	If so, was the wreck due to the failure of the department to provide a proper light at the end of this jetty, and is the vessel a total loss?
3.	Is it a fact that the said jetty has been without any light for three months or any other lesser period and that there is no mark or communication at the end of the said jetty to show the entrance to the channel of the north arm of the Fraser river.
4.	Has the government a report on the wrecking or grounding on or about Thursday, March 15. of three tugs with booms of logs at a point on Sea Island about one mile east of the said jetty?
5.	Has the government taken steps to provide a proper and sufficient light at the end of the said jetty and to otherwise properly protect the entrance to the said channel for navigation ?

1. The Department of Marine and Fisheries has received a report of the wreck of the Trader.
2.	The vessel was stranded 300 yards west of the jetty at noon on March 16th during what the captain in charge described as a furious W.S.W. gale. Consequently the wreck was not due to the absence of a light.
3.	The edge of the channel is 400 feet from the jetty. The department has maintained since 1905 range lights to mark this channel. The outer light was carried away on January 21st last by the tug Gleeful, the report of which did not reach the department until January 31st. Instructions to rebuild were wired February 2nd.
4.	No.

On the Orders of the Day:

I would like to draw the
attention of the government to a report which has appeared in the press recently to the effect that complaints have been made in England, by importers of grain shipped from the port of Montreal, that the shipments were short in weight, and that a commission is likely to be appointed by the government here to inquire into this matter, and to ask the government whether they have received this complaint, and if so, will a commissioner be appointed to conduct an inquiry?

The attention of the
department was called in December last to a complaint which had been made by the directors of the Liverpool Corn Trade Association respecting a shortage of grain shipped from the port of Montreal. The matter was taken up with the Harbour Commission of Montreal, and an officer of the department was entrusted with the task of making an investigation. We are convinced that if there is anv shortage, no blame can be laid on the port "of Montreal. We sent the report of the investigation to the High Commissioner of

Canada in London, who transmitted it to the Liverpool Corn Trade Association. The latter are not quite satisfied because that investigation was made by a department of the government. They want a more impartial investigation, so to speak, and that is what the High Commissioner has stated in a letter written to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. We have answered that we regret that this investigation has not satisfied them; but as the matter is very important, we are going to see that another investigation is made under the Inquiries Act. I am actually considering this question in conjunction with the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Let me add that the harbour commissioners of Montreal invite the investigation; they will be only too pleased that it should be made, and, indeed, they were prepared to carry it out themselves. They contend that if anything is wrong, it is not on their end of the transportation process. An announcement will be made shortly.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair:
Railways and Canals-Chargeable to income-To increase the amount of loan authorized by Vote No. 136 Main Estimates, 1922-23-Additional amount required $13,099,493.34.

Mr. Chairman,-
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Acting Minister of Railways and Canals):	Might I oe
allowed just a word? I believe my hon. friend who has just risen to his feet, desires to discuss this item. I would suggest to the committee that after he makes his remarks, we allow the item to stand, as several other hon. gentlemen have told me that they wish to make some observations on it, but they are not prepared to do so to-day.

I am fortunate in having this early opportunity, before speaking directly on the question before the committee, of congratulating the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). I do so with great satisfaction, because I am aware of the capabilities of the new Minister of the Crown and especially his capacity for work. He has-and this has a direct bearing on the appropriation which we are now considering-an intimate knowledge of the railway question. He knows, in an unusually thorough manner, many of the difficulties which exist in connection with railways. His presence therefore, in the cabinet is additionally satisfactory, because I think he will bring to this question a well-founded knowledge and a sympathetic attitude, which I believe

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
are not evident in the cabinet at the present time. During the debate on this appropriation, some discussion as regards the question of railway policy and transportation has been raised. The importance of the discussion was increased by the statements of two members of the government. Their statements were of importance, and at the same time their remarks were, I. thought, of a dubious nature and of a disquieting character.
I wish to review, to some extent, the situation as regards the railway system and the railway policy. A few weeks ago the Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), in the general summary which he presented to parliament, made some very important statements. He informed us that there were 22,646 miles of National railways. He also told us that the value of these 22,646 miles as appearing on the books of the various companies, amounted to $1,892,577,750, and further that the total earnings in the year 1921 amounted to $233,789,000. These are a few of the outstanding features of the very large organization which the country now possesses. This property was handed over to the Canadian National Railway Company by order in council of the 20th of January of this year, and that order in council entrusts the National Railways of Canada with the keeping of the Canadian National Railway Company for its management and operation. The only limitation in this connection is the proviso that it shall be during the pleasure of the Governor in Council. Up to yesterday no further copies of orders in council had been tabled showing that any subsequent instructions haye been issued by the government to the Canadian National Railway Company. In other words, the government has passed over to the company the railways for operation and management without any instructions or any indication of what is to be done, or any general outline to be followed. Nothing of this kind has been done at all. There appears to me to be. a striking lack of policy on the part of the government when it hands over this stupendous system of 22,000 miles to the company for operation and management without some guidance or anything to indicate in a broad way what the views of the government are. I ask, would anyone, in any other form of business outside of government control, contemplate handing over a property of this enormous importance and of such huge wealth to a company's management informing that company simply to go ahead and operate the business, without at the same time laying down some policy that shall be followed? Can anyone think of such a thing in connection
with a matter that affects the financial condition of the country to such a large extent?
The property was entrusted to the company under a statute entitled "An act to incorporate the Canadian National Railway Company, ^and respecting Canadian National Railways." The company took over the railway more especially under section 11, and I shail read this to the House:
.... the management and operation of any lines or railways or parts thereof, and any property or works of whatsoever description, or interests therein, and any powers, rights or privileges over or with respect to any railways, properties or works, or interests therein, which may be from time to time vested in or owned, controlled or occupied by His Majesty, or such parts or part thereof, or rights or interests therein, as may be designated in any order in council, upon such terms and subject to such regulations and conditions as the Governor in Council may from time to time decide; such management and operation to continue during the pleasure of the Governor in Council and to be subject to termination or variation, from time to time in whole or in part by the Governor in Council.
The authority, then is given to the government to invoke such regulations and conditions as they think proper in entrusting the railways to the company. Where are these regulations and conditions? So far as can be ascertained from the orders in council no regulations or conditions have been laid down and passed on from the government to the company. The government have taken no such position in this matter. But while the government have not seen fit to give any general directions to the company in the way of guidance, certain commitments have been made on behalf of the country, and there are. conditions which have existed for some time that bind the government to lay down certain broad and definite principles which the company shall follow. Among these commitments, I might refer first of all to the Intercolonial Railway, which is a matter that is often mentioned in the House. It is mentioned, frequently I think, without any very definite idea of what the British North America Act says on the point, and I therefore propose to read the section of that act, which is not long. Section 145 of the British North America Act says:
Inasmuch as the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, have joined in a* declaration that the construction of the Intercolonial railway is essential to the consolidation of the Union of British North America, and to the assent thereto of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and have consequently agreed that provision should be made for its immediate construction by the government of Canada: Therefore, in order to give effect to that agreement, it shall be the duty of the government and parliament of Canada to provide for the commencement, within six months after the union, of a railway connecting the river St. Lawrence with the city of Halifax in Nova Scotia, and for the construction thereof without intermission, and the completion thereof with all practicable speed.
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

We are quite aware that different views are held regarding the construction which this section entails, and without taking anything more than a moderate view of the section and what it calls for, I believe that it is fair to assume that it does show that this was to be a public undertaking essentially and that it was not necessarily a financial or commercial enterprise. I would suggest therefore that on the face of it this is a government railway and stands in a different relationship from other railways in the country; and I contend that it is not open to this government or parliament to dispose of it to any private corporation if that were proposed. The other fair deduction, I think, is that the conditions attaching to this railway are such that it is incumbent upon the government to see that trade between the Maritime provinces and the rest of Canada shall move freely and without any undue hindrance. But during the last few years this has not been the case, and this fact has been one of the grievances which have been complained of. So much then for the Intercolonial.	.
Now, how does the country stand in connection with the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific? This House and the country generally were given to understand when the measures were before Parliament that these two railroads would be used for the encouragement of Canadian trade from east to west and from west to east. As emphasizing this understanding I shall quote section 13 of the act of 1911 respecting aid towards the construction of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway. By this section it is declared:
That the aid herein provided for is granted by the government for the express purpose of encouraging the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. Before such aid is granted the Governor in Council shall require the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company to enter into an agreement undertaking that all freight originating on the line of the Canadian Northern Railway Company or its branches, or on the line of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise bv the shipper, shall, when 'destined to points in Canada be carried over the Canadian Northern Railway, or the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway, or the connections of either of them or over any railway within Canadian territory; and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports; and that the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company shall not in any matter within their powers directly or indirectiy advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall, in all respects, in good faith, use their utmost endeavours fMr. MacLaren.l
to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
As further emphasizing this understanding I shall now read three paragraphs-42, 43 and 45-from the act of 1903 respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific. This act will be found as chapter 71 of the statutes of that year, and it is interesting to note that it was signed on behalf of the government by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). Paragraph 42 is in these words:
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for poilnts in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
Now paragraph 43:
The company further agrees that it shall not. in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall, in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely,-the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
Then the last paragraph bearing on the point is additional to what I have read in reference to the Canadian Northern. I refer to paragraph 45:
The company shall arrange for and provide, either by purchase, charter or otherwise, shipping connections upon both the Atlantic and Pacific oceans sufficient in tonnage and in number of sailings to take care of and transport all its traffic both inward and outward, at such ocean ports within Canada upon the said line of railway, or upon the line of the Intercolonial railway as may be agreed upon from time to time, and the company shall not divert, or so far as it can lawfully prevent permit to be diverted to ports outside of Canada any traffic which it can lawfully influence or control upon the ground that there is not a sufficient amount of shipping to transport such 1 raffle from or to such Canadian ocean ports.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it may be said that while there is no evidence of the government having drawn these commitments to the attention of the railway board, still the latter are 'supposed to be aware of the legislation.' Personally I do not think this suggestion is satisfactory. The property is too large and valuable and of too much importance to the country for us to depend on mere supposition. The existence of these commitments should be made clear to the country generally and

Supply-Railways-C.N.R.
to the railway board in particular, and that, I conceive, can only be done by order in council.
I need hardly say that these undertakings or agreements were known generally by the public at the time the legislation confirming them was enacted. Indeed, the country was not content to grant such generous aid to these railway companies unless, in return, the railway companies gave these undertakings so that the whole Dominion would be benefited, for the real object of building these railways was, through the encouragement of trade within the country, to ensure national prosperity. These are the commitments, and they must be lived up to. I am not saying that the government do not look upon them as commitments, but we would like to hear something more specific in the matter. In any case, those conditions are there, and as a matter of right, as a matter of good faith, they should be fulfilled.
I wish now to refer to the question of the transportation of Canadian products through United States ports and the transportation of American products through Canadian ports. It has frequently been stated that a large amount of Canadian grain is transported through United States ports, and when you look at the figures furnished by the Bureau of Statistics you cannot help being doubly impressed with the truth of that statement. In the year ending March 31, 1921, there were exported through the United States 58,839,270 bushels of Canadian wheat and principal grains, as compared with 48,401,141 bushels of Canadian grain exported through Canadian ports. In the year ending March 31, 1922. the amount exported through United States ports was 99,301,421. bushels, and through Canadian ports, 69,239,823 bushels. For the period ending January 31, 1923^the March figures are not yet available-the amount exported through United States ports was 160,250,892 bushels as compared with 88,232,899 bushels through Canadian ports.
. Mr. CLARK: How much through the port of Montreal?

I think I have the figures for Montreal and for Vancouver as well, but I would like to follow up this general line for the moment. While the respective amounts exported through American and Canadian ports vary somewhat, the figures show that 65 per cent, or even more, of our Canadian grain is exported to countries beyond the seas through the United States. That, I say, is a very impressive statement, and one that is not calculated, I think, to satisfy the ambitions ol Canadians.	.
I would like to refer briefly to the matter of flour. The amount of Canadian flour exported through United States ports for the year ending March 31, 1921, was 1,546,714 barrels as against 3,282,568 barrels exported through Canadian ports. In 1922 there were exported through United States ports 2,864,699 barrels of Canadian flour, and through Canadian ports, 3,979,016 barrels. For the period ending January 31, 1923, the amount exported through American ports was 3,696,144 barrels, as against 5,496,963 barrels exported through Canadian ports. So that so far as flour goes, while a vast amount is exported from Canada through United States ports, the proportion is less unfavourable than it is in the matter of wheat and grains.
I have heard it stated in this House that while an undue amount of Canadian grain is being exported through American ports, that export is offset by the amount of grain that goes from the United States through Canadian ports. Well, these are the figures: For the year ending March 31, 1922, the amount of Canadian wheat and principal grains exported through United States ports amounted to 99,300,186 bushels as compared with 79,693,438 bushels going from the United States through Canadian ports. This shows a considerable preponderance in grain exported from Canada through United States ports over the amount that is exported from the United States through Canadian ports. It therefore cannot be said to be an offset. It is a partial offset, but it is far from being a complete offset.
I have other figures here. For the 'nine months ending December 31, 1922-the figures for the last three months are not available- Canadian grains passing through United States ports amounted to 146,210,694 bushels, as compared with 91,838,301 bushels of United States grains passing through Canadian ports, showing a very large preponderance for nine months in favour of the American ports.
For the year ending March 31, 1922, there were 2,864,699 barrels of Canadian wheat flour exported through American ports, as compared with 104,385 barrels of American flour exported through Canadian .ports, or something like twenty times more Canadian flour was sent through American ports than American flour through Canadian ports. I have a similar statement for the nine months ending December 31, 1922. For that period there were 2,307,676 barrels of Canadian flour sent through American ports as compared with 12,046 barrels of American flour sent through Canadian ports. Those figures, I think, are very striking. It is hardly

necessary to emphasize the point that one of the most important articles of production in this country is grain, and that this is very largely exported to a foreign country. These figures show that this country is not sharing in one of our important industries, namely, transportation, to the extent it should. This question of transportation is of the greatest possible importance, not only for the government to consider but the Railway Board as well. It concerns both the government and the railway company and must be considered not only from the general point of view of the transportation of Canadian business over Canadian railways and through Canadian ports, but regard must also be had to the formal agreements that have already been made governing a considerable portion of the railway.
In answer to my hon. friend from Burrard, the amount of Canadian wheat exported via Montreal for the year ending March 31, 1921, was 28,298,040 bushels.
Was that all wheat?

The figures I have given are headed " Quantity of Canadian Flaxseed, Barley, Oats, Rye, Wheat exported to Overseas countries via Canadian seaports direct." It states that the total of wheat and other grains exported for the year 1921 was 37,008,373 bushels: for the year 1922, 52,320,740 bushels, and for the year 1923, 60,098,995 bushels. Those are the figures given to me by the Statistics Bureau. I have given this information simply in answer to a question and it does not bear quite on the point I was bringing up.
Now we come to that part of the railway question of which we heard a good deal yesterday, and that is that portion of the Grand Trunk which runs from Montreal to Portland, Maine, and as regards the business that is now being done by the Dominion govem-
4 p.m. ment through the port of Portland, Maine. At the present time the difference in distance between Port Arthur and Portland, and Port Arthur and St. John, New Brunswick, is 253 miles in favour of the Portland route, that is, if the route is taken from the short cut at Long lake and the freight carried from McGivney Junction through Fredericton to St. John. One offset to this 253 miles, and there are several offsets, is the difference in grade in favour of the Canadian route. The grade of the Grand Trunk from Montreal to Portland, Maine, is one and one-fourth per cent. The grade from Port Arthur to St. John over the largest portion of the road is four-tenths per cent;

I am advised that that is the case for all except twenty-seven miles, and that is an important offset. It means that a full freight train can be carried from Port Arthur to St. John continuously, whereas if the freight was taken from Port Arthur to Portland, Maine, the freight would have to be divided in Montreal and sent on in two trains. That is an important offset. There is this other factor, and that is that when the wheat goes through St. John or Halifax the money is spent in this country, and surely that is an important offset. The business is there. The railways can do the business. They are not so congested that they cannot carry on until the traffic is forced out via the Grand Trunk to Portland, Maine. Therefore, it is a question with the railway companies and with the government whether they think it advisable to raise a certain amount of money by dividing their business between Portland, Maine and Canadian ports, or concentrate on having the main revenue derived from our own Canadian ports. Difficulties are arising, no doubt, in the situation, but are they sufficient to deter us from making the best arrangement we can, rather than accepting the easier course of least resistance? While one does not wish to appear in any sense as a railway expert, in all railway matters, as in everything else in life, there is a tendency to follow the path of least resistance, the rut so to speak, the custom of doing certain things, is apt to be followed, and it takes a vast amount of determination to follow a newer and a better method.
Some figures were given, in answer to a question not long ago, regarding the business done in Canadian grain through the port of Portland and through the port of St. John, and I wish to have these figures incorporated in Hansard. The amount of Canadian grain carried to Portland, Maine, since October 1, 1922, by the Canadian Government railways, was 14,756,808 bushels. The amount of grain that was carried through St. John by the Canadian Government railways during the same period was 1,706,376-fourteen millions and three quarters to Portland as against one million and three quarters to St. John. The amount of United States grain that was brought to St. John during the same period was 367,282 bushels-a comparatively small amount. The Canadian Pacific railway brought 11,047,981 bushels of Canadian grain and 2,202,121 of United States grain to St. John. The amount taken to Halifax was reported as nil. A certain amount of grain is brought from the United States to St. John but the amount is small in comparison with

Suppl y-R a il xva ys-C .N.R.
these amounts, particularly the amount sent to Portland, Maine, over the Canadian National. Here is a fact that I think the House might well consider: That at the present time the Canadian National Railways are taking to Portland, Maine, over 14,000.000 bushels as compared with one million and three quarter bushels to St. John.
I need hardly say that that matter is not entirely satisfactory to people who live in the Maritime provinces. They are showing very great concern and very much dissatisfaction with the conditions that now exist, and I would impress on the government that it is most desirable, not only in the interest of the prosperity of the country, but also in the interest of the contentment and happiness of the people, that this unsatisfactory condition should be changed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) made a statement yesterday in reference to the situation. To my mind his remarks were very disturbing. He said in part-
Mv lion. friend has forgotten that by the action of the government of Canada in acquiring the Grand Trunk railway, we have acquired another Maritime port at Portland, Maine.
Let me see if that be the case. The late
government was more successful than were the commissioners in the drawing up of the Ashburton Treaty. They never succeeded in acquiring Portland, Maine-far from it-and yet the Minister of Finance says that the late government acquired another Maritime port in Portland, Maine. I think it is a most important thing. Mr. Chairman, not to confuse the issue. Having a railroad from Montreal to Portland, Maine, does not constitute having a port at Portland, Maine. It is confusing ideas. But the Minister of Finance is not given to confusion of ideas. He is remarkably clear, I do not think he has taken a dispassionate view of the situation or he would hardly advance that proposition.
Is it not correct to say that the late government acquired a railroad to Portland, Maine?
That is what I am saying. My hon. friend is quite right. I said acquiring a railroad was not acquiring a port at the same time-especially a foreign port.
Acquiring a railroad in this case implied acquiring a terminus of a railroad, which was Portland.
I think what I said was quite clear and what the Minister of Finance said is also clear. He said a port.
I say that too.
And I say that is a confusion of ideas and a confusion of the issue. It is not acquiring a port, and I am pleased to have the opportunity of refuting that statement.
Instead of "acquiring," what is the proper word?

I will answer the question of my hon. friend if he will remain quiescent for a little while. The minister stated as reported in Hansard:
We have acquired another Maritime port at Portland, Maine.
Acquiring a railway from Montreal to Portland is, in my judgment, a long way off from acquiring a port; it is also a long way off from compelling the government to make use of that port whether they have a terminus there or whether they have not. There is in the act nothing laid down that I know of compelling the government to maintain that port, or to see that traffic goes through Portland, Maine. The minister went on to say:
The question is an ugly one, and this complicates it. We own the Grank Trunk railway, and Portland is the Grand Trunk railway terminus. This is the problem we are giving to Sir Henry Thornton. We are asking him to make these roads reasonably profitable, remunerative, self-sustaining.
Where is the official record of this request that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) states has been made to the railway board? He stated:
We are asking him to make these roads reasonably profitable, remunerative, self-sustaining.
I have pointed out already that there is no order in council giving any instructions whatever to the railway board, beyond entrusting them with the property and empowering them to operate and manage it. If Sir Henry Thornton has been asked to carry on this road, as the minister stated yesterday, so as to make it reasonably profitable, remunerative, self-sustaining, I should like to have the record. The minister went on to say:
We give him this road to Portland. Is he to let that road be idle, to let the rails get rusty, or to try to send some traffic over the Portland road in order that it may contribute something towards the cost of the system ?
That seems to me a method of conducting an argument that is not convincing, that is not satisfactory to this committee. What is the use of talking about rustv rails? I am afraid we have enough of them in this country already, and I do not know that the minister is exercised about, that. But we know there is trade originating in Chicago, and it is carried to Portland, Maine, over the Grand Trunk. Nobody raises
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

any dispute over that. Nobody says: "Do not do that." On the contrary, vve agree that it is right and proper to carry that on. There is passenger traffic going on between Montreal and Portland, Maine. Does anyone wish to represent that nothing but wheat is going over that road? We know to the contrary. Wheat, of course, is not going there in the summer. That is not a method of conducting an argument that we might have expected; but in any case, if the railway is there and if the terminus is there, outside of all that I have mentioned, is that any reason why a government or a railway board should wish to keep up a foreign port at the expense of our own port? The business can be done as well, as cheaply, and I believe with more financial benefit to the country by sending the traffic through Canadian ports.
When this matter was discussed prior to the last election, a tremendous hubbub was raised about the taking over of the Grand Trunk.

If the figures we were given in my home town, Barrie, were correct, between eight and ten million dollars worth of equipment was presented to this country by the Imperial authorities after the war. This equipment came to Camp Borden in carload lots, and it did not cost this country a cent of money, except possibly some transportation charges. Hence, the plant is undoubtedly extensive there and also up-to-date, I am led to believe. Apart from assembling, transportation charges and the percentage that was paid by Canada for these extensive buildings constructed by the Imperial authorities, we are getting ail this for nothing. I would think, before the department seriously considers establishing new plants, they would make very sure that they are going to save money by so doing, because there is no question there is ample room for expansion at Camp Borden.
If possible, I would like the minister to verify the figures I have given regarding the equipment which came out from England and which was presented to Canada, and, if it is not amiss, I should be glad to know what was paid. I have heard different figures mentioned. I heard it suggested first that the buildings at Camp Borden were offered to the Canadian Department of Militia at fifty cents on the dollar. I heard later that the figure was reduced to 25 cents on the dollar and that is, as a matter of fact, what was paid. I do not know whether this information is private. If it is, I do not want to pry into it. But if it is not, it might interest the members of this committee to know that these buildings were secured at this small figure. In any event, I am quite certain they were secured at a substantial reduction. When the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mew-burn) was minister, the matter was then under consideration, and I cannot say whether it was under his regime or that of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that the actual deal was made. If it is proper to get the information, I should be glad to get it now.
I can only say, in conclusion, that if a.ny members of this House have an opportunity of visiting Camp Borden, they should do so. They will find there one of the finest camps in existence. I have heard that from men who have seen the finest camps in the world. There is everything there. The property was acquired by this country at twelve dollars an acre, and I doubt very much if any deal was ever put through by the government of Canada where property was ac-

quired at so low a rate as was Camp Borden. You have abundance of opportunity for artillery practice. You have the buildings for anything you want to go into. You have no end of cement pavements. You have a wonderful sewage system. You have the finest water you can get anywhere in this country. Two or three artesian wells, eight inches in diameter, supply this water. There is practically everything that could be wanted at that camp. The only thing I could criticize is the matter I mentioned to the minister yesterday. The approaches there are not what they should be; they are not fair either to the men or to the public who are interested in the camp and who have a right to visit it. The cost of this improvement would be only a nominal matter; these approaches should be made right, and if that is done, we have at Camp Borden as complete a camp as could be wanted by anybody.

I am speaking from memory now. Those buildings were acquired at a comparatively small cost to the country. This is one of the departments of the public service upon which I think the country can congratulate itself. This is the only opportunity afforded hon. members to offer some constructive suggestions in regard to the present postal service, especially the outside service, and I shall take occasion now to refer briefly to some matters which I consider important. In England, in the United States, and in Australia the governments have restored the pre-war postage with the result that there has been a large increase in business. I do not think that there is anything that retards the growth of a country and hinders its trade and commerce more than the imposition of high postal rates. The report of the Postmaster General of Canada discloses the fact that the Canadian people are being taxed through the postal service and that the surplus revenue over expenditure for 1920 was over $3,000,000. The postal rate in Canada was three cents prior to 1897 when deficits were being rolled up every year in the Post Office Department. Sir William Mulock then introduced the two-cont rate, and although
the deficit was not converted into a surplus at once, nevertheless in 1902 a surplus was secured which has increased year by year, unbroken even by the war. I may remark, also, that in the United States the war tax on postage has been dropped and a great increase in the postal service of that country has resulted. The boards of trade and chambers of commerce encouraged the government, and while it was thought that the reduced rate would not be satisfactory there was a huge surplus last year; and I observe from the bulletin of the National City Bank, an important corporation, that this reduction has done more than anything else in the United States to restore confidence in business not only of the retail men but of the wholesalers and of the farming community as well. The same thing has been the experience of the Mother Country. A tax on the postal service of a country is a great discouragement to trade and commerce and the British Postmaster General has brought down an elaborate statement this year in which he reckons upon a surplus of over $46,000,000 for the current year, of which $37,500,000 will be devoted to a reduction of post office charges including postal rates overseas as well as domestic postage particularly. With that surplus they are not only giving the staff higher salaries but they are reducing the postal rates to other parts of the Empire.
In regard to postal receipts, I need not refer to the city which I have the honour to represent, for its pre-eminence in volume of postal and customs business is well known. Yet although the postal receipts reach the huge total of over $5,000,000 we cannot get a new post office. I would commend to the government the example of Sir William Mulock, who with his courage and foresight reduced postal rates and made the Post Office Department a paying institution, converting its recurring deficits into surpluses year after year. It must be remembered that this is a department of government in which the people are very closely interested for they are directly benefited by low rates of postage. It may be said that to reduce our postage rates to the pre-war basis will mean a loss of revenue, but, Mr. Chairman, I predict that as in the United States and England such a great volume of increased business will follow lower rates of postage that still greater surpluses will result.
To-day the Post Office Department is doing splendid work and its officials throughout the country have the confidence of everyone and by their devotion to duty notwithstanding the comparatively small salaries they receive they have given us a demonstration of the success of public ownership. I would urge the gov-

Supply-Post Office

ernment to go further and, like the British Postmaster General, extend the scope of the operations of the post office. Por example, in England the Postmaster General is utilizing some of the surplus on the installation of radio equipment, better rural mail delivery and the reduction of the rates on all kinds of postal matter including drop letters. Undoubtedly the time has come when we too should reduce the rate on such letters.
I have before me a statement of the postal receipts by cities for the past twenty years, and in view of the large receipts from the city of Toronto I would ask the hon. minister if something cannot be done now towards providing a new post office building which is so badly needed. True, we have a post office in the new union station, but a new central postal building is immediately necessary.
By a courageous and foresighted policy on the part of the Post Office Department, such as the reduction of postal rates to the prewar basis, business will be encouraged and stimulated, better wages will be possible for the post office employees, and the Dominion generally will be benefited. Such a policy I am confident will command itself to the wisdom and judgment not only of the three parties in this House but of the country at large.

Mr. Chairman, taxes are unwelcome anywhere. In the realm of finance I would not care to trespass without having consultation with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and I am not sure that he would, without a good deal of consideration, consent to our dropping this form of taxation-because that is what it is, taxation on behalf of war expenditures. It is quite true, as my hon. friend says, that what was done some years ago led to an increase rather than to a decrease in the revenue of the Post Office Department, but whether a similar course should be adopted now is a matter for consideration.
I can assure my hon. friend that the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) has been talking very frankly on many occasions to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) to the end of securing further postal buildings in the city of Toronto. Not being Postmaster General, perhaps I can talk more freely on this subject. It does seem to me that a big centre like the city of Toronto in which such a large volume of postal and customs business is conducted should have facilities of the very best for the carrying on of such business. However, that is a matter for discussion. I can assure my hon. friend that I will report what he has

said to the Minister of Public Works and the government for consideration.
My hon. friend referred to the salaries of, I imagine, our letter-earners and so forth. In this connection he will be interested to learn that the Post Office Department has inaugurated a new system which will be of some benefit to the department itself and will give permanent employment to men -who heretofore have had but temporary employment. For instance, taking the city of Toronto, during what I might term rush seasons, or when the permanent employees were absent, quite a number of men were employed to fill their places temporarily, their services of course being dispensed with when the regular employees returned to duty. Under the new system instead of having the employees take their holidays .within a limited period they will now be extended over ten months of the year, so that temporary employees who are looking after the duties of those absent will have constant employment. That is one reason for the increase in the estimates this year.

I should like to take this opportunity of saying a word in behalf of, in my opinion, the most underpaid branch of any service of the government, namely, our rural mail carriers. For perhaps four or five years there has been an agitation conducted on behalf of these men. Something has been accomplished for them, but very little. I well remember in 1919 a change was made, and at that time I interested myself to the best of my ability in their behalf, believing that they were absolutely entitled to consideration. At that time it is true that prices were rising, and as many of these men had entered into their contracts when the prices of oats, horseshoeing and other things incidental to their work were not so high, they found themselves in a very awkward position, being bound by contracts on which they were losing money and from which there was no escape for four years. They pressed for improved conditions, and I should like now to put upon Hansard a letter which I then wrote on their behalf and which, while not altogether appropriate at the moment, is so in the main. I still express the hope that the amendment I then urged upon the Postmaster General may still be introduced, together with another change in the system to which I shall refer later. My letter to the Postmaster General bears date the 11th September 1919 and is as follows:
Dear Sir,-Pursuant to our conversation I am writing you on behalf of a numb'er of rural mail carriers who made complaint to me that they cannot make a living on the remuneration they receive, and in my opinion their contention is unanswerable.

Supply-Post Office
Many of them receive from $500 to $700 a year, and for this they have to keep up either one or two horses, buggy, cutter and harness, or motor, and while not working all day are nevertheless on the road every day but. Sunday, rain or shine. I have asked the Superintendent to authorize a reasonable increase but he tells me he cannot; and I understand nothing can be done except cancel the contracts and call for new tenders.
I would like to suggest that the act be amended giving the Postmaster General power to grant a reasonable increase in proper cases. The amendment might provide that no contract should be reconsidered which has not been in force for at least one year. It might further provide that no increase exceeding say $100 or $150 a year, at the outside, should be made without new tenders. In my opinion such an amendment would save the department a large sum of money each year so long as prices continue upward.
It may be argued that the carrier is treated fairly if the contract, which he finds onerous, is cancelled, but that is not so in many cases, for he has his equipment which involves an outlay of from $250 to $500,-
These figures are very moderate; perhaps they should have been a great deal higher.
-and rather than sacrifice it he plugs on dissatisfied and disgruntled, and pours out his woes to all on his route, and they join the shout, knowing beyond question that he has in many cases, just cause to complain.
When one stops to reflect what a street car conductor or city postman receives,-
I would like the minister to understand that I am not offering any criticism of what they do receive; I merely refer to their case for the purposes of comparison.
-or when a comparison is made with the salary or wages paid in almost any line of business, the rural mail carrier is found to be in a class by himself.
I mentioned that the amendment asked for would save the department a large annual outlay. This will be explained by reference to many cases with which the superintendent is familiar, where a reasonable increase of say $75 to $150 has been asked and refused for want of authority, and in the end the new contract price has involved an increase far exceeding the amount which the carrier asked, and the expense of advertising has to be added as well.
I am not directing attention to recent contracts but to those made 18 months or more ago.
I sincerely trust something may be done at this session.
Sincerely yours,
(Sgd.) W. A. Boys.
What I suggest to the minister, and what I press upon him for consideration, is an amendment to give the Postmaster General the power to make increases in the remuneration of rural mail carriers of from $100 to $150, putting upon it whatever limit the minister thinks proper. Let us just consider the question for a moment. We find there is a contract in existence. The carrier has satisfied those on the route. He has his equipment; he has been doing the work for four years; nobody wants a change. So far as I know, the department is willing to renew the contract if the carrier will continue at the same rate, but if he is able to show that he should have some increase, even only to the
113i
extent of $25, the minister now has no power to award the contract on that basis to the man who has been doing the work satisfactorily and who has the equipment for properly carrying it out. It must be readvertised at considerable cost, and I venture to say that in most cases the lowest of the new tenders received far exceeds the old rate plus the small increase that the carrier asked for. It may be objected that to give the minister that power would place upon him or upon his superintendent a responsibility that he should not undertake. If the suggestion involved $500 or $600 per contract, I could give way to that thought, but when it is limited to $100 or $150 it seems to me that that objection is not sufficient to stand in the way.
At the time that letter was written, as I have said, a change was made; the contract was cancelled at the request of a man who claimed he was losing money, and he was let out. That was the extent of the relief he got.
Now, time has not improved matters. The work of the carrier has been increased. He now has to handle registered letters; he has to sell stamps; he has to take care of the parcel post. His responsibility is greater. The public enjoy this service; I believe it is the best thing that was ever done for the farming community and even if an improved system did cost a little more the farmers are entitled to it and should have it. They appreciate it, but as they use it more constantly they naturally become a little more exacting and look for greater efficiency. The demands made upon every carrier are therefore greater, but the remuneration remains practically the same. Let us make a comparison or two. What is the system in vogue in the United States? There they adopt the uniform system of $75 a mile, and the position is a permanent one so long as the work is properly performed. Why should not some such system be adopted here? The only objection I have heard to it is that there is a variation in the routes; one route is harder than another, and for that reason such a basis of remuneration might not work out fairly. Well, it must work out fairly in the United States or they would not have adopted it there. It is true that upon some routes the roads are better than upon others, but as a rule where you have these better roads you have a more congested population and more work for the carrier to do. From there you go to the routes where the roads are not as good and where the carrier has less work to do, so that one condition would counterbalance the other. I suggest, therefore, the consideration of a rate per mile for this service. I am not saying what it

*
Supply-Post Office
should be; that is a matter for the department itself.
Again, comparing what the rural mail carrier gets, with what the city carrier gets I understand that the salary of the city carrier runs from $1,335 and upwards per year. They receive clothes; they get three weeks' holidays; they get ten legal holidays, and they get bonuses. The rural mail carrier works six days in the week, every week in the year, rain or shine. He has to provide himself, I venture to say, with two horses on every route that runs over 15 or 16 miles, and the average length of route, I am told, is 20 miles. I do not think any carrier can cover a route of 20 miles every day in the week except Sunday unless he has two horses; in the summer time, as a rule, he has a motor. He does not get a single holiday. He does not get the three weeks that the city carrier does, or the legal holidays, or the clothes, and no bonus or help of any kind. The average pay of the rural carrier in Ontario is $816 a year, or $2.60 per day; the average in the Dominion is $7o0, or $2.39 per day. So far as I know, the lowest wage of a labouring man, who is even provided with a shovel, is from $3 to $4 per day. But the mail carriers have to provide their own equipment and perform the service from day to day without holidays; and they cannot get people to relieve them. Surely they are entitled to- consideration.
It may be said in reply that if any mail carrier wants to quit or if his contract expires and the position is advertised, you can find somebody who is ready to take his place. I ask: Is there a single office in the gift of the government-and I make no exceptions in respect to which, upon its being vacated and the position advertised, the place of the occupant of that office could not be filled for less money than he is getting? But after all, is that the proper test? I admit that when these contracts are re-advertised, in some cases-by no means in all-you can find men who are ready and willing to perform the service for the same money, in some cases even for less. When they undertake it, they do not know what they are up against; they take a chance on it and as a result the public suffers. I think that in this service as in all other branches of the government departments we want to secure efficiency, if possible, and the reasons given, I think, answer the tender and contract suggestion. I urge, therefore, in all sincerity, that some change should be made.
Make it the union rate of wages.

My hon. friend makes a suggestion about the union rate of wages. Well, we find that method creeping in everywhere. I am not making an appeal on that ground at all. I am making it on the ground of merit, and the gross underpay which, if continued must lead to inefficiency. Why should the work of these men and their responsibilities be increased from year to year and no extra remuneration be given? How can you get men to do the work properly and satisfactorily if they feel they are underpaid, if they feel that another man performing the same service a few miles away from them is getting more? A man may take a contract at forty or fifty dollars for four years supplying bondsmen. He may have taken it too cheap. Perhaps a month or so afterwards he finds a carrier about ten miles distant is getting sixty or seventy dollars. These are not dreams. I know carriers in my own riding where there is a great difference in the renumeration of the men, but no difference in the work they perform, no difference in the routes they travel. Now to satisfy these men I would suggest that they be put upon a par. If the country cannot stand what is being paid in the United States, $75 a mile, perhaps it should be made less. I do not know for certain what the carriers themselves are urging upon the government, but I have heard it placed at $70. It seems to me that that can be gone into, and when it is gone into a reasonable allowance can be made.
I see it is nearly six o'clock and I do not feel that anything can be gained by asking that the House should now rise, because I think I have said concisely all, at all events that I can think of. It does seem to me that the reasons I have advanced are reasons which should commend themselves to the sympathetic consideration of the department. I am glad to know that the matter is in the hands of the Acting Postmaster General, the Minister of Militia. I believe him to be a reasonable man, a man always open to persuasion so long as your arguments are good. How can anyone suggest for a moment that these men should go on doing this work for $2.50 or $2.60 a day when carriers in the city whose hours are no longer, I think, get practically double the pay and do not have a horse or motor to keep up, and in addition are provided with clothes and get the holidays I have referred to? How can you expect efficiency from rural carriers under such circumstances? They have to go out in the morning and break their own roads in the winter quite frequently, and they are criticized if they do not manage to get

Supply-Post Office
through, because the people who are expecting their mail are dissatisfied if the carrier does not arrive on time with the mail. I have no doubt the minister's office is full of letters of criticism when as a matter of fact the carrier could not get through on account of bad roads. Nevertheless some of those living upon the route are dissatisfied and make their complaints.
In conclusion, I would most earnestly urge these matters upon the attention of the department. I know they have been pressed by the carriers themselves, but like everything else I suppose it requires a little extra pressure to make the change. I think the time is now ripe for the consideration of a change which will give these men a rate of pay commensurate with the importance of the work they are doing and with the responsibilities they have to assume.

How much of the amount voted last year under the heading " Mail service by railway, $7,899 " was earned and paid to the Canadian National system and the Canadian Pacific Railway respectively?

I am sorry I have not that information for my hon. friend. I will give the House the general policy of the Post Office Department. As Acting Minister of Railways, I would like to carry all the mails on the Canadian National; as Acting Postmaster General I may say the policy is to use as far as possible the Canadian National lines, but the general policy is to use the most expeditious means of transportation, the getting of the mails to their destination promptly being the chief characteristic of this service.

Does the
minister know of territory in Canada which is served by both systems where the service is practically the same and where the privately owned railway gets the mail contract?

I would not go so far as to say that, but where the Canadian Pacific steamer brings the mail across the ocean, it expedites the service of the Canadian Pacific steamer to give its own mail .train that is waiting there on its own track the carrying of the mail, and this mail would be carried to all parts of Canada on the Canadian Pacific rail wav.
Has the Canadian Pacific Railway the contract, or is there any contract between the railways and the Post Office Department for the carrying of the mail?
There is no contract. The Post Office Department pays the railways for the space used.
And they can select the trains for them?
Yes.

Just before the recess I was pleased to hear the remarks ot the hon. member on my right (Mr. Boys) with regard to the position of the rural mail service carriers in the Dominion of Canada. I think the remarks which he made fit the situation absolutely. In my constituency I have had numerous complaints from rural mail carriers as to the payments they receive and with regard to other matters, especially dealing with the contract system. That system, as it is carried on is, to my mind, a very vicious one. It gives us a class of public servants that are very poorly paid. In fact it works out very much like this; that the cheap men, or the men who will work for a low wage, irrespective of their ability to do the work, are the men who get the contracts. We find that the average mileage which the rural mail carriers cover in the Dominion is about 19i miles, for which service they receive in the neighbourhood of $42 per mile. I think no one here will argue that that is adequate pay for the work they do. They have great expense to bear. For instance, they have to provide a suitable rig for the purpose, they have to maintain that rig, and we all know that it is a very difficult and costly matter to maintain a rig which is on the road during the summer months and travelling on all kinds of roads. That amounts to a very considerable portion of their work. Then they have a horse to maintain. They have to get blacksmithing done, furnish their harness, and pay for the feed of the horse and it amounts to a very large sum, so that these men do not get a living wage. Making a comparison of the wages of the two classes, the position of the rural mail carriers is very much worse than the position of the city letter carriers. The average wage for the city letter carrier is $1,335 per year. I do not, wish to be understood as saying that these men are getting too much; in fact, I think they are not, but when you compare the compensation, the comparison is not favourable to the rural mail carrier. I think the government should take
Supply-Post Office

this question into consideration. I am satisfied that the poorest paid body of men in the whole government employ are the rural mail carriers. I think the time has arrived when we should improve the postal ^service of the Dominion. I understand the postal department had quite a surplus last year-the only department in the government that showed a surplus-and I think it is up to the postal department to improve the postal facilities as soon as possible. We find there has been practically no money spent for a good many years, owing to the war and other causes on the post offices throughout the Dominion. In view of the fact that we have a surplus on hand at the present time, the government owes it to the public to take steps immediately to introduce a better system of post offices that will meet the needs of the people of Canada in this regard.
Is it the intention of the government to continue the bonus to the letter carriers during the coming year?

I think the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance has an estimate now before the House for the continuation of the bonus as it was last year or approximately so. All classes that were covered in the former year will be covered this year.
As regards the wages of the mail carriers in the country, of course they are not paid wages. These are not men working by the day or the month; they are contractors; they are given the rate which they tender for themselves. I am not a great lover of the tender system in many ways. Of course I would probably stand almost alone if I were to get up in this House and state that we should do away with the tender system. I would not go that far because this system is a protection; but in some of our services at least, I know money is not made by adhering rigidly to the tender system. It, however, seems to ensure more than any other system the protection of the public. These men are contractors, and while some of them are pretty poorly paid, that is to a large extent their own fault, because they tender for these services and they sign a contract. Moreover, a contractor has to give a bond to ensure that he will do his work, and if he does not do his work properly, the bond is forfeited. The question is worthy of discussion; but we do not want to get mixed up in our minds mail carriers in the cifies and towns with mail carriers in the country. In the cities mail carriers devote all their time to this work, and they are paid so much as civil servants. In the country many of them are not occupy-

ing all their time in this work; they do other work as well, and they are doing this work at a price fixed by themselves and not by the department at all.
I have a great deal of sympathy in regard to the small rate at which many of these men perform their work; but supposing we took the view of the hon. member for Sim-coe (Mr. Boys). At the present time, as the law stands, any contract, the amount of which is over 8200, can be renewed at that figure; but if it be increased, new tenders must be asked. Supposing it were left to the minister to increase a tender, would not hon. gentlemen detect quite a line of patronage in that? Would not the minister, whoever was in power, be accused of exercising patronage? Bill Smith says: "I will do this work for $700." The minister's friend is carrying the mail, and the. minister would hav? power, if we were to change the act, to give the contract to Tom Jones for $100 more. Thus the question is surrounded with difficulties. This would afford the minister an opportunity to exercise patronage for his friends, and perhaps the House, when it came to consider the matter, would not think it wise to give him that power. How else would you fix this? The hon. member for Simcoe says: "Pay so much a mile." The system in the United States is different from ours, because to begin with they are far advanced over us on the question of good roads, and a mile is a mile in a large portion of the United States because their roads are practically all good. Supposing we took nineteen or twenty miles of road that is clay, and we have a mileage rate of so much for the mail carrier. The man on the clay road will get the worst of the deal, when he has to traverse the route in the fall or spring. Then there are sections of Canada where horses are not used in the winter. In sections that are comparatively small automobiles are used. In the riding that I represent, the mail carriers for the most part use automobiles; the roads are good, and mileage in the greater portion of my riding would be on an equal basis. But where our roads are as they are in the Dominion, some good, some bad, the latter predominating, it would be most difficult to fix a mileage rate that would be applicable to all parts of Canada.
Personally I would like to see the mail carriers better paid; but will somebody tell me just how that can be worked out without giving the government of the day patronage that perhaps hon. gentlemen would not think- they ought to have? Of course at the present time this would be perfectly safe; but there might come a time when it would not be as safe,

I listened with considerable interest to the answer of the minister to the suggestions that have been made and I noted his reference to patronage. I hope he will
not object to the proffered confidence which I was willing to repose in him and his department in this connection. I do not think it would be misplaced; at least, I trust not. Now, I do not think his argument will bear investigation, although to a very slight extent perhaps he is right. I would ask him to bear in mind that in the first instance the contract is let by tender, so that the situation we would have to deal with would arise when the contract expired at the end of the four-year period. The minister or his superintendent would then be confronted with a request on behalf of the particular carrier for an increase, and I have suggested that the increase should be limited. I would say that it should not exceed at the outset $150, or perhaps $100. But with that very slight increase a carrier could be satisfied. It would not be patronage, because he got his contract in the first instance by competition in which he was the successful tenderer. For my part I would be perfectly willing to trust either the acting minister or any minister or superintendent to do what is fair to the extent I mention, and that would obviate the necessity of advertising. The carrier would have to show reasons why there should be an increase and I am satisfied that the country would save money if that course were followed. The only argument advanced by the minister against an even rate per mile for the service as between the United States and Canada is that in the United States the roads are more uniform and are better than in Canada. I do not agree with him there. Perhaps he has seen more of the roads in the United States than I have, but I may observe that I have travelled over a number of them. I am ready to admit that the state roads in many of the states are superior to any rural roads we have, but these routes do not go over the state roads only, they form a very limited part of the mileage of the United States; and on the side roads I want to tell the minister that from the limited experience I have had in travelling in the United States, the side roads there are worse than they are in Canada.
I keep off the side roads when I am across the line.

That may be, but unfortunately we have a lot of farmers living on the side roads in Canada and if. is on their behalf that I appeal, because they must be served. I had the pleasure of spending a little time in Florida last January and travelled over a good many roads there, and I can say that the roads in my hon. friend's county and in my own are vastly superior to the roads I travelled in that Btate. There are many roads

As I said before, the farming community are entitled to this service; and indeed they are delighted with it; it is the best thing that has been donoi I want to urge the minister therefore to keep up the standard of the service. Do not let it be depreciated by some of the methods that have been followed. We know what those methods are. Now, I am not criticizing the minister at all in saying this, because the idea is to get things done as reasonably as possible. At the same time, I do not approve of the methods. Tenders are called for; they are received and are considered too high. An inspector then goes to the locality and he not only goes to those who have tendered and does his best to bring them down, but having the benefit of the information the tenders disclose, he scours the country to find someone who will do the work for less. Finally he gets some man who really does not realize what is before him, and perhaps in a moment when he is pressed for work he undertakes the service. The carrier who has been doing it before and doing it properly, being fully equipped, and whose son perhaps has been helping him, finds all his equipment left on his hands. If you get down to an even basis per mile you will overcome that trouble, because a man will get the work at a fair price and he understands that he can retain the job if he does his work properly, but not otherwise. Surely under these conditions you would get better results. If what I Bay about the American roads is right, that answers

we want to treat our Canadian National Railways as a business concern which will get business on its merits from the public of Canada. My hon. friend asks me a question. I should like to add a
word to what has been said on behalf of our rural mail carriers. It is not sufficient to say that this is an old question that crops up every year, or that we have a system of contract which must be the best simply because we have it. The fact that these complaints recur periodically show that the system is not what it should be. And undoubtedly these complaints will continue until the system is put on a better and fairer basis than obtains at the present time.
I represent a rural district and am familiar with the conditions under which these mail carriers work. I have taken considerable pains to go over their rounds with them and to estimate approximately what they are getting for the work performed. In two or three cases a few years ago, with the help of the department here, some of these men were released from their contracts under which they were unable to make a living, and allowed to tender again on a somewhat improved basis. But since the conclusion of the war this practice has not been continued.
I entirely agree with what has been said by the two hon. members who have so ably dealt with this subject, but I want to add my view of why the contract system does not work out satisfactorily as applied to the carrying of our rural mail. This is another case where theory is very beautiful but fails to work out in practice. The reason is that ordinarily any government work done under the contract system appeals to a class of business men who know exactly the conditions under which they are tendering. But our
rural mail service is a comparatively new service and appeals only to a very limited class of people in the country districts owing to the low rate of wages allowed under the contract, and these men, because of lack of education and business training, have no adequate idea of what is involved when they sign the contract. In addition to that, just as has been already stated, departmental officials who are paid a living wage spend their time in many cases drumming up people in the country districts to tender at an extremely low rate in order to save the department the difference between this and a fair rate, although the wages of these officials is costing the country enough to pay the mail carriers a living wage. So it is really not economy to induce men to sign such contracts.
Another unsatisfactory feature is that under this system men are engaged to deliver our rural mails at the lowest possible remuneration without any regard whatever to their ability to discharge the duties required of them. I am not sure that I would entirely condemn the system of handling our rural mails providing the tenderers were required to pass an examination to prove that they possessed the necessary education to enable them distribute the mail. Under the present system we find rural mail carriers who are scarcely able to read, with the result that mistakes are constantly made by them, important mail is delivered to the wrong address, and in some cases serious financial loss occurs. Certainly we should have efficiency. To my mind it is folly to talk of investigating conditions of unemployment and underpaid workmen while the Dominion government in its system of rural mail contracts conducts one of the worst sweatshops in the country. If these carriers had to show certain qualifications, those qualifications in themselves would enable them to determine a fair rate of remun-eratidn under their contract.
If the contract system is so good, why do we not apply it throughout every department of government. I think if we had our cabinet ministers- and all others engaged in the government service paid under contract the evils of the system would be impressed on the people in a very decided manner.
Then again if a rural mail carrier has rendered good service under his contract it should be renewed as it expires and so encourage him to continue to render the most satisfactory service possible. I think it has been stated by at least two hon. members that under the present system a man can retain his contract at the same rate of pay. I do not know what the arrangement is, but I can point out what

has actually happened, which is much more important. On one particular route of about twenty-two miles the contract recently expired. On the last occasion of its renewal, when prices of everything were rather high, the contractor secured the contract at $1,100, which is at the rate of $50 per mile, or $25 a mile less than the American government pay its rural mail carriers. This man is one of the most efficient carriers in the service. He has a wife and family to support and devoted his whole time to his route. His work was eminently satisfactory, being almost entirely free from mistakes. One would think that such an efficient public servant would be retained in the service. When the time came for renewal of his contract he was so fair-minded that he allowed for some reduction of living expenses and actually offered to continue the contract at a reduction of $100, although he had to keep two horses and the necessary equipment to carry out his work; but for some reason or other the contract was advertised and was awarded to another man who may not possess the excellent -qualifications of his predecessor. The new man secured the job at $800. This instance I think clearly indicates that the practice referred to of allowing the tenderer to continue his contract does not always obtain; and I may say that I know of other cases of a similar nature. Why could not an arrangement be made to continue satisfactory men in the service instead of going to the expense of advertising for fresh tenders. I have no doubt that the man who has contracted to deliver the mail at $800 will be a dissatisfied servant and similar cases are what give rise to the continual complaints which we receive with respect to the rural mail service. Surely the government can devise a system under which efficient service can be secured by paying at least a living wage.
This is what it means, that on the average, each rural mail carrier has a twenty-mile route which he has to cover six days in the week, and to do this work it is absolutely necessary for him to keep two horses and the necessary equipment. On the most conservative estimate this cannot be done for less than $300 a year. Assuming the average carrier gets $750 under his contract, this leaves him only $450 to support his wife and family-$450 for working six days in the week throughout the entire year. Can anyone say that this is a credit to the country? And it is only possible to get men to enter into such contracts because they are not sufficiently conversant with business principles to know what rate they should tender at in order to ensure to themselves a fair wage. They only find out their mistake by bitter 
experience. I am convinced that if tenderers were required to pass an examination to test their efficiency the undesirable element would be eliminated and those who passed would be able to command a living wage. If you provide in some way that the man who proves his efficiency is not in danger of losing his job for the sake of a paltry $25 by being underbid by a man who may not be able to show that same efficiency, then you have done away with a good deal of the cause for complaint. As to the flat rate per mile, I am fairly well acquainted with most of our Ontario roads, and after careful consideration I have come to the conclusion that a flat rate would be very fair to all concerned. In almost all cases the better roads have the heavier class of service; there are as many complaints from the mail carriers with regard to obstruction of traffic on the really good roads as there are respecting the back concessions where the' roads are not so good. So that the one balances the other, and the adoption of a flat rate for this service would not be a very serious injustice to anyone. It would, I believe, be entirely satisfactory to the men themselves.
Would you give that flat rate without any tender?

Well, I am not suggesting that; I am pointing out what is wrong. I say we should either retain the contract system and provide for some examination, or adopt some plan whereby a man who proves himself efficient will not lose his job if he is getting a reasonable rate of pay, say, not less than $50 or $60 a mile. If his contract is not for more than that, surely he is entitled, in view of his good service, to keep his job. The people cannot be contented in the rural districts when they learn that other men working for the same government in the cities are treated differently, in that they receive a bonus-the continuance of which appears to be necessary-are given the benefit of pension provisions, are supplied with clothes, etc. On the other hand, the poor fellow in the country is working at starvation wages and has to provide everything, including the upkeep of two horses, and has left for himself not more than $450. That a man should have to work under those conditions and attempt to support a family should surely appeal to right thinking persons as an injustice that is no credit to this country or to the government, and that ought to be remedied without delay. The present government, I believe, is especially sympathetic to the workingman-or at least, they
