were prior to the last election. Possibly owing to the pressure of business their plans in this respect have been mislaid. But I do hope they can now be utilized on behalf of the rural mail-carriers of Canada.

As one who represents the largest rural constituency in Canada, I would say that I have no sympathy with any person who will tender for a job and then, after he has got the work, start in to whine and ask for a raise in salary. I believe in the contract system. It is the only fair system, it is the only way the taxpayers of Canada will get a square deal. If you put it in the hands of the Postmaster General to the extent of $150, it will simply mean this: A person may tender for a small contract at $150 less than he really wants to get; then he can go to the member representing that section of the country and pester him until he gets the Postmaster General to make that increase of $150. A good deal has been said about starvation wages and cutting the rates to the rural mail carriers. I can call to mind one instance out in my district. During the war a man had a contract for carrying the mail at $1,850. He said he could not make it pay at that rate, and he tried to hold the government up for $2,500. The government called for tenders-that was in 1915-and one man tendered at $1,175. He got the job; he is still carrying on the work and is perfectly satisfied. If tenders had not been called on that occasion the taxpayers of Canada would have been held up for $2,500. It is urged that some of these contracts are very small. Well, I know of one instance where a man had a contract to carry the mail twice a week a distance of six miles, at the rate of $3 a week. That did not look very much, but what did it mean? A little girl of his got on a cayuse in the morning before going to school and went down and brought the mail up. It was simply pocket money for her. If anybody else had tried to get that contract from him, why, there would have been a regular row over it. On the other hand, if it were left to somebody to put a value on the delivery of that mail and somebody came in from outside to deliver it, the cost would probably be $25 a week, and even at that the amount would not be considered too much. As for keeping up a plant to carry this mail, in the rural districts they do not maintain very much of a plant. It is generally carried with a surrey in the summer and an old sleigh in the winter; it is the ordinary plant that they had before they took the contract. I believe in calling for tenders, and I believe that if those who tender have not brains enough to put in a proper price for a job then they
should go under and let their bondsmen go good for the default. That is the only way the taxpayers of this country will ever get a square deal.

I am of the opinion that no real injustice is done to the rural mail carriers through the contract system. I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. McBride) that if a man wants to make a contract at a low price there should be nothing to prevent him from doing so. On the other hand, a great many of the rural mail carriers are none too well paid- many of them are underpaid-but they are rendering good service. I do not agree with the suggestion presented by one hon. gentleman in regard to holding an examination for the position of rural mail carrier. The position is not one that requires any very high standard of education. It does not require many of the qualifications that other occupations require; nor does it require the upkeep of pure-bred horses. But it does require men of sterling qualities who are not afraid to face storms and bad roads and all that kind of thing. I do not know that there is anything seriously wrong with the contract system, unless, as I have heard it stated, it is that when a man puts in a tender at a figure which is sufficiently low, some of the authorities persistently endeavour to get someone else to take the contract at an even lower price. I do not think that is proper. If a tender is honestly made and the price is not exhorbitant, the contract should be given to the lowest tenderer provided he is able to furnish the necessary securities. But there is another phase of the question that is of great importance; that is, the legal holidays. I think these men should get the legal holidays. As one who is served by the rural mail carriers I think I am safe in saying that the farmers and the rural population generally will not suffer if these men have a holiday now and then. To give them that concession would ease their minds and make them feel that they were getting what other men are getting elsewhere in similar positions. It is hardly fair to ask them to go over all kinds of roads in all kinds of weather every day in the year except Sunday. The government should take that matter into serious consideration. In fact, I have been taking the matter up with the department with a view to bringing about that change. I wrote to the previous Postmaster General on more than one occasion, but the Post Office Department take the ground that a contract is a contract. Truly a contract is a contract, yet I believe these men should be granted the legal holidays or the major portion 'of them at least, so that they could have a little rest

I think that would help the situation and make it easier to secure contractors for this work, for the lack of holidays has been a very serious complaint among all the rural mail carriers with whom I have come in contact.

Can the minister give the

That is a question that
has been engaging the attention of the department. While I am not in a position to make any statement I can say that the department has been seriously considering what ways and means it could use to extend the service. The amount that is being asked for here is for services already under contract. The service in

some cases may have been extended a mile or half a mile or something of that kind, but this vote is not for opening up any new territory. The condition in the prairie provinces cannot however, exist very long, and I can readily understand, although it would probably mean quite a deficit, that possibly a portion of the discontent of which we have heard might be allayed if the people of the West
9 p.m. had a rural mail delivery to bring them closer together, and give them closer connection with the outside and with the centres. I am not in a position to make any promises. It is very unsatisfactory to , those people living in well settled communities to see the mail deliveries in the towns and other communities, when they cannot have the same privilege. When I go to the department I am always told that they are not establishing any new routes in any district. I have taken that as an answer, and have always advised the community interested that no more routes were being established at the present time. I think it would look more reasonable if someone else were allowed to take this money, intead of raising the salaries of those who are already carrying the mail. It would look better if the department would allow more routes to be established at rates at which people are willing to carry the mail, rather than to raise the wages of those who have contracted to carry the mail at a certain price. I would not be in favour of raising the remuneration above the amount for which these people are willing to carry the mail, but I am anxious to see more routes established in localities where there is no service now. The cities have the delivery now, and it is not so much trouble for any one living in the city to go to the post office and get his mail, as the families living in the country have to do. I think it would be well for the department to consider the establishment of new mail routes in places where there are sufficient settlers to justify such an expenditure. However, I believe that we must all be tolerant. I believe that we are using too much money in the service not in the Post Office Department alone so much as on all lines of Government service in every way throughout the whole country,

and that we are spending more than we are justified in spending or can afford. However, when others are receiving these services it seems hard on communities who are not able to get them, and, therefore, there is considerable dissatisfaction. As the minister has said, country life would be more tolerable, and I believe it is worth while in Canada to undertake to make the farmers feel that they are getting consideration and service for the part of the taxes they are paying. I think the government is justified in giving all the service to the people however, that we can pay for. It struck me that it would not look well in the eyes of the people in these communities I have been referring to if the wages of the mail carriers were raised above the figure for which the carriers were willing to carry the mail.

Speaking of the rural mail service, I am not particularly objecting to the contract system. I practically agree in the presentation that my hon. friend and neighbour from South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) made to the House this afternoon and tonight. At the same time the chief objection I make to this contract system has reference to what is often done in connection with it by officials of the department. This feature was illustrated by my hon. friend and I know what he said to be the fact because the practice complained of has been resorted to more than once in my own immediate neighbourhood. I take strong exception to that kind of thing being done by government officials. I refer to the practice of a government official going out after the contract has been sent in, and beating down this one and that one, in order to get the wages to the level at which the contract is finally awarded.
I would like to see the rural mail carriers given the statutory holidays, at least. They should have those holidays, especially Christmas. to themselves. I am willing to do without my Christmas mail, in order that the men who have been carrying my mail to my door for 313 days each year may have a holiday, and I think the people in the rural districts generally would also be willing to dispense with the Christmas mail. I suggest that that matter be taken into account when tenders are being asked for by the department, either for the renewing of old contracts or for making new contracts.
I am not going to argue to-night in regard to the question of raising the price paid to the rural carrier, but I would like to see a little more equality than we have at the present time in the delivery of mail, whether letters or other articles, in rural and city districts. Some

time ago an answer was given to a question asked by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Elliott) in regard to the salaries paid to the rural carriers and those paid to the city letter carriers. There is a great difference between those salaries, and I took the trouble to figure it out on a per hour basis, because of the answer that was given. The answer was that in the one case it was for service which varies as to time occupied daily, semi-weekly-, etc., and in the other case it was for full time service. I recognize that there is a consideration there. On the other hand, we ought to consider that, while the rural carrier perhaps does not give all day to the service, his day is broken into, and the balance of the day does not amount a great deal to him in the matter of earning. Take our own case; the train comes in some time about ten o'clock and the mail carrier starts out. His forenoon is broken up. He cannot go out and do a half day's work He gets back at five o'clock in the afternoon and his afternoon is gone. It is not fair to put it on that basis. If we figure this out on the per hour basis, we find that what they get per hour is about 35 cents. The city mail carrier gets about 60 cents per hour, and I understand he gets, at least, two uniforms a year. A man who is carrying mail in the rural districts, if you figure out the amount he gets on the same basis, receives a reward, or a salary, or a wage, if you like to call it that, of 38 cents per hour, while he is actually in the service of the government or in our employ. For that 38 cents per hour he also furnishes a horse and rig which are absolutely necessary. Some system should be evolved whereby that inequality could be overcome.
I do not know just why the one should be on the contract system and the other in the Civil Service with the contract system eliminated. The latter is a permanent official, and his salary is, I understand, based on the cost of living. In the other case, the salary is fixed on the basis of what some other fellow who, perhaps, does not know what he is-undertaking, says that he is willing to perform the service for. I know very well that a bond has to be signed or bondsmen procured that the contract will be fulfilled. It is not fair to put the rural mail carriers on that basis. We talk about the merit system in our Civil Service, and this eliminates the merit system. Let me put the question in this way. A man who has filled a four-year contract satisfactorily has an opportunity of renewing that contract, if he so wishes, at the same price. I think that is generally the rule, although an hon. member to my right seems to find that this rule is not always carried out. At the same time, however, there is no recognition of

the faithful service that the man has given. These are some of the disadvantages which we have at present under this system. I am not too sure whether I am prepared to subscribe to the mileage basis or not. There are some very good features in it; but there are other features which I do not think would be in the interest of economy in the service. There is one feature to which I strongly object, namely, that of government officials going out, after tenders are sent in, and beating down, as it were, persons who are offering to do the service. I hope that practice will be discontinued.
There is one little matter that I resent. In talking over this situation with some of those who are interested, I might go so far as to say, with some who are officials of the Post Office Department, I was told that the trouble is that in rural districts too much service is given. As one of those living in rural districts, I thoroughly resent that statement. We get a mail service once a day in our district, and that is quite sufficient for us. The mail service in Ottawa, is, I believe, twice a day, and I am not prepared to accept the statement that we are getting too much service at the present time, particularly when such a statement comes from the department itself.

I have for some years watched the rural mail carriers on the one hand and the city mail carriers on the other, and I have wondered if some fairer adjustment could not be made regarding the remuneration of these two classes of public servants. I happen to live in the country on a back road where we have had to shovel the mail carrier out time and again. People livting along that route will expect that man to deliver the mail, and they will raise a row because he does not deliver it on days when it is impossible for the people themselves to get along the road. That condition is common in the winter season in that section of the country. When I come to Ottawa, what do I find? I find a man receiving $500 a year more for delivering mail on city streets where he does not do as much work in a day as the rural mail carrier does. The trouble seems to be that in the one case the government can fix the price, but in the other, it must be let by contract.
I happened to have some difficulty last session and I have also had it this session in connection with rural mail carriers in my constituency. The report which I get from these men does not correspond exactly with the statement of the minister to-night. They tell me-and I am almost forced to believe there is a great deal of truth in what they
state-that even where a man who has been doing his work satisfactorily, puts in his tender, the department are not satisfied, but they send out men to beat the price down to a lower figure by almost any means possible. Why cannot the department cut somewhere else and give the rural mail carrier a fair show in the way of remuneration for his services in comparison with what men in the Post Office Department are getting? Why should he be discriminated against, when men in other branches of the Post Office Department are getting something more nearly approximating what they ought to receive? I do not say that any of these gentlemen are getting any more than they ought to get; but the mail carrier in the rural sections is certainly not getting what he ought to get. In these estimates I see a whole column of increases. I do not understand what these increases mean. Why should the salaries of these Post Office officials be increased? Why cannot some of the money be given to the men who carry the mail in rural Ontario, the western prairies, and, perhaps, in the eastern provinces, and let these Post Office officials do with a little less pay, because even if the salaries of the latter are cut down, men can be got who will do the work efficiently?
We were speaking about immigration in this House for several days. We expect a rural mail carrier to carry mail for one-half-* or a little less, I think it is by the report this afternoon-of what men are getting across the line for carrying the mail there Does the government expect to keep men in the rural sections and prevent them from going to the cities and towns, when men in the urban centres are receiving $500 a year more than they do in the country? These are some of the things I cannot understand, and I feel sure, if the department get busy, the}' can give these rural mail carriers a little more money to which they are entitled and also the advantages that were asked for by other hon. gentlemen this afternoon. I meet these men every day; I have to go home and report to them, and I cannot sit quiet in this House while this debate is going an without expressing my opinion on the matter. These men ought to get fairer treatment from the department than they are getting.

Undoubtedly the
rural mail carriers should receive more than they do. We all know the work these men are doing for a small salary. However, it does not seem to me that we should cut down the salaries of any of the mail carriers, whether of the city or the country; rather there should be a decided increase in the salaries

A few months ago we had here in Ottawa a convention of all the postmasters, at which the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) paid a most eloquent tribute to the work of the postal carriers. I took from the paper at the time an extract of what he said, and it seems to me that he was only doing justice to the men whose services we all require and appreciate. May I read a paragraph:
Of all those engaged in bringing the postal service into the lives and homes of the Canadian people none fills so large a place as that familiar figure-the letter carrier.
There is something stirring and wonderful about the relation of that faithful figure to the daily lives of millions of our people. He is a part of a vast business which can be tabulated in terms of annual turnover, and number of employees, and curves of profit and loss, like any other business, but which is, nevertheless, the strangest, most human and most romantic business in which men were ever engaged.
Now, we all realize the great service performed by these men and yet I think we mu*t confess that there is a very Slight chance of definite promotion for a large number of them. Very early in life they reach the maximum of their earning capacity. In a great many other walks of life men can proceed to higher salaries and better positions in every

way, but that is impossible for the great majority of the letter carriers. Now that there is a surplus reported in this department of the government service, I think it would be only reasonable for us to increase the salaries of the postal employees all along the line until they are comparable with the salaries paid in other lines of business. As I think I said a year ago, in my own city of Winnipeg last year there were people in the receipt of relief from the city of itself who were receiving more than the employees of the government who were carrying on a very important part of the public service. Again, may I ask that we have some sort of assurance that in the not distant future there shall be a general revision upward of the whole of the salaries of the postal employees?
My hon. friend makes a statement but he qualifies it at the end. It was not the same at the end as it was at the the beginning.
Possibly at the end I stated where I stood in the matter and what my hopes were.

My hon. friend said that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had stated that in the near future there would be a revision of salaries, but in his remarks he slipped in the word "upward", which might materially alter the meaning of the Prime Minister.
I did not suggest that the Prime Minister had promised a revision of salaries upwards. I was merely expressing the hope that in any revision that might take place these salaries would be increased.

I think it not altogether out of the re^lm of probability that there will come a time very shortly when the bonus system shall disappear. That being so, I suppose that the revision of salaries on a permanent basis will be made when that system is discontinued.

This government has been in power now some fifteen or sixteen months. During that period we have had no direct declaration from the government with respect to the question of the repeal of the Civil Service Act, and I presume that they are waiting upon the report of the special committee which is now investigating the matter. But while they are waiting I make the statement deliberately that in so far as the Post Office Department is concerned they are violating the spirit of the Civil Service Act if not the letter on every occasion that presents itself. On

Too bad.

I say the Post Office Department is deliber- , ately defying not only the letter but the spirit of the Civil Service Act in withholding the installation of Mr. Potter as the postmaster at Clementsport. I say further that it is violating both the spirit and the letter of the act in order to cater to a local partisan spirit and put into office the former postmaster who was dismissed for political activity by, I presume, a former government. That

is to say, the law is being violated in order to perform an act of partisanship. Oh, oh.
I want to tell hon. members opposite that we cannot trifle with the returned soldiers. They are entitled to these positions if they are competent to fill them. ,
In my riding our predecessors put in a very strong party man when a returned soldier was anxious for the position.

Then I hope the veterans will go after it again. They did not do it very successfully at that time, but there will be opportunities later. In the Clementsport case Potter is entitled to the position. If the government can convince the Civil Service Commission that he is not a resident and that that debars him
notwithstanding the fact that he is a returned soldier, if they can convince the Civil Service Commission, all well and good, but that is the court to which they must go. They are not in appeal over the Civil Service Commission, they are not there to see that the commission is carrying out the law in each individual case. If they were, there might as well be no Civil Service Commission. If the government has the power to listen to one of its supporters who says that the Civil Service Commission did not do right because Potter was not a resident, and therefore can put another man in office, that is only another way of repealing the act, and let me repeat, they are repealing it in the Clementsport case, and they are doing it in numerous cases 10 p.m. in Ontario. They are spreading patronage all over this country and doing it very frequently in defiance of the prior rights of the returned soldiers.

My experience is very different from that of hon. gentlemen to my right. Since I have been elected a member of this House I have been asked several times by the government to nominate someone for a postmastership where the remuneration would be under $200, and in every notice I got to that effect I was asked to give returned soldiers the preference. I got notice of one postmastership being vacant the appointment for which really came under the commission, and I was a little perplexed to know why I had been notified. The vacancy was at a point fifty miles from where I reside and I only knew one man there. I forwarded the notice to him and told him that evidently the government wanted someone nominated, and for him to choose a fit and proper person. He wrote back and told me that on the very day he got my letter an agent of the Civil Service Commission came to that town and asked him to nominate someone, and a party was chosen who was afterwards appointed. I have had I think, seven vacancies for the position of postmaster in my riding, and as I said before, in every case the Civil Service Commission asked that a returned soldier be given the preference. So far as I could see, everything was done fair and above board.
But I know that when the late government was in office a Liberal who was keeping a post office where the income was over $1,000 took a very active part in an election campaign, and he expected to get his walking papers, and he did. In the West, so far as I know, things have been done pretty straight , in connection with the post office service.

I just wish to say a word as to what my hon. friend says. He says he
Supply-Post Office

has been asked to nominate postmasters where the remuneration is under $200. I do not doubt, that that is correct although I must say I have not received any favours of that kind myself. Evidently hon. friends to my left have a degree of affinity that I do not possess with the government of the day.
Hear, hear.

What I want to call attention to is this. That does not in the least affect the classes of cases we are speaking of here at all. The Civil Service Commission has nothing to do with that class of case.
I quoted one case where it had.
Was a returned soldier recommended?
The notice said that a returned soldier should get the preference.

That is the act. The Civil Service Commission was doing its duty, and it did the same in the Clementsport case. But the government stands in the way and refuses to let the law take effect. Undoubtedly the commission always does that, and let me say further, in western Canada I do not think there is very serious complaint, and I think I know the reason. In western Canada there is not, and has not been for some time, the same patronage Spirit as to office that there is in other parts ox Canada. Western Canada has been in favour of the Civil Service Act and this system for years, and it is in favour of it to-day, and that applies, I think, to members of all parties in western Canada. It does not apply to individuals by any means, but western Canada almost unanimously is against patronage, and the government will get no support and no encouragement whatever in that country for anything in the way of an invasion of the Civil Service Act. But it is wholly different in Ontario. It is wholly different in the eastern provinces. In those provinces in the case of positions of some value to the returned man, the government has time and again consistently made it the practice and policy to evade and even defy the Civil Service Commission. I do not know what value a $50 position or even a $150 position is to a returned man.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition asked the hon. member for Digby and Annapolis (Mr. Lovett) to mention names.
Yes.
Will the right hon. gentlemen give us some names.
Yes, I will give you the case of the Wingham post office.
Let us have the details of it.

The details have been
published. I will give the hon. gentleman the references. If he will read the press of western Ontario in September last, or the Veteran of that month, he will get the Wingham and the Brussels cases and a great many more, that will harrow his soul, if he has any respect for the Civil Service Commission.

I have listened with considerable interest to the remarks of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) with reference to the government evading the Civil Service Act and sitting in judgment on the Civil Service Commission. He has referred to matters occurring in western Canada. I do not know so much about western Canada, but I come from eastern Canada, where the post office authorities employ very many men indeed, and I found, to my sorrow, on many occasions that it was utterly impossible to get the government to evade the Civil Service Commission in any way.
Why is the hon. member so sorry?
Well, I will leave it to my hon. friend himself to make up his mind. He will know why as well as I do.
The hon. member wants a government that is a law breaker?

Not entirely. I am only refuting what my right hon. friend said a few minutes ago, and I refute his statement absolutely as regards the city of Montreal. I will also say that the returned soldier, in my experience and to my knowledge, is invariably given the preference when he has an opportunity of filling the position. I have never come across a single case in which I have made application to the Postmaster General, or to any of the authorities in Ottawa, that I have not been referred to the Civil Service Commission, and I have always referred applicants to the Civil Service Commission. I have found it perfectly useless to do anything in any of the departments of the government, excepting through the Civil Service Commission.

I have been reading the
Mirror, and I am pretty well posted now. However, 1 only want to say a word with regard to western Canada. I have seen no

Supply-Post Office
signs of any of those deeds in regard to which accusation has been made to-night, as far as patronage in western Canada is concerned. I have listened to the remarks made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition. I would be very sorry, indeed, if they were true, and I think the members on this side of the House anyway would like a little more definite and accurate information that the Civil Service Commission has been set aside by any action of the government. I hold no brief for any one, as far as that is concerned, but I would be very sorry indeed if the Civil Service Commission were being ignored by the government in making appointments. I have no knowledge whatever of anything of that sort having taken place, but at the same time I would not condone any offence along that line.

An hon. member of the Progressive group has just made a confession that he has been consulted with regard to the appointment of certain postmasters. That, to my mind, is being privileged to handle a certain portion of patronage. I hope that is not a general practice on the part of all the Progressives. If it is, the onus is on them to ray so now, or forever be silent. Personally, I have not had any opportunity, nor am I desirous, of handling any such patronage, and I respectfully hope that all the Progressives are not handling patronage in that way.

Perhaps I may come in the class of those who are privileged, but I want to make it clear that I am not here in any way to screen our government. On the other hand a little reference was made to me in my own constituency, where I was asked to recommend a man to take charge of one of those post offices, to come in under the $200 class, and I recommended a man who was a returned soldier. If the committee want to get the actual facts, the man I recommended had originally been, and perhaps was then, as far as I know, a Conservative, but I recommended him to the Postmaster General at that time, and he was appointed postmaster, and is postmaster now.
What was his salary?

He was under $200.
But I want to be fair to the government, and I say that in that case they did what was right by the returned man, although he was a Conservative.
What does the poor man do for a living, with a job in which the salary is under $200?

He is a blacksmith
and has a good trade.
He would need it.

I am going to enter a
very emphatic protest. It seems to me, so far as the present government are concerned, they are discriminating against me, because I have never been asked to make any recommendation for postmaster or anything else.
No vacancies.

Yes, lots of vacancies,
I would like to get back to the question we have been dealing with, with regard to the transportation of the mails on the railroads. I have before me the report of 1922, and I ndtice the daily mileage of postal cars in March 1922 was something like 71,928. Now can the minister give us information as to the number of postal car miles for the different railways in Canada?

My hon. friend is asking me for some detailed information as to the postal car miles which I am unable to give him. They have never been asked for in the House on any occasion. I never dreamed that any such question as that would enter into the discussion. It is a detail that really has not very much bearing on the question that he is trying to get at. I can readily see that that would be followed by another question. I have not that information. It has never been given in the details in the postal estimates. I sent out for information after the hon. member had spoken. I do not want my statement to be taken as absolutely accurate, but, as far as the official could estimate, he believed the mail canying was divided between the two great systems in the proportion of about 45 per cent to each, and the other systems about 10 per cent. That is what my hon. friend is trying to get at directly, I think.

Yes, that is quite true.
I suppose the minister will bring that information down in order that we may perhaps have some more accurate statement. Could the minister give us any information with regard to the number of rural free mail deliveries in the various provinces of Canada?

They are not divided by
provinces, but the rural mail routes in number and operation are 3,742, and the number of boxes erected 200,027. The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) was asking those questions. The approximate cost per year is $2,771,203.54. We do not have them divided
Supply-Post Office

by provinces. I think my hon. friend can take it for granted that the rural mail routes are largely in the East and not in the prairie provinces.
Do I understand the minister to say that the rural mail delivery routes are mostly in the East and not in the prairie provinces?
I said I thought the larger number of them were in the East and not in the prairie provinces.

I do not know about other constituencies; but I take it that the situation in them is the same as it is in mine. During the last year we have had many requests for rural mail delivery routes, and in every single case, so far as I know, the request has been turned down by the government. Is it the intention of the government next year to let up as regards this matter, and to give the rural people some opportunity of getting their mail delivered?

I dealt at quite some
length with this matter earlier in the evening, when my hon. friend was probably not in his seat. To be frank, I may say that there is in this estimate nothing to provide for any new routes. Expressing my own opinion, I believe the time must arrive before very long when the rural mail system will have to be extended. I am speaking particularly of the West and expressing my view in the absence of the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy), who would be in a better position than I am to discuss this. As I said an hour or so ago, rural mail delivery, rural telephones and roads -all this kind of thing helps to make a contented people in a rural district by bringing them closer to each other as well as into closer touch with the great centres. That is a question of great import, and speaking for myself, I think the time will soon come when the rural mail route of Canada will have to be extended for these purposes, as well as for the accommodation of people living in rural districts. These things all tend to make not only people in sparsely settled districts more contented, but those districts more attractive to other people who might wish to come into them. The United States has extended a somewhat different system, and the deficit there this year is about $60,000,000. The question is altogether one of expense, how much the country can afford and how fast it can go.

Last year when the Post Office estimates were under discussion, I asked the minister for a statement of policy

as to what the department proposed to do in connection with extending the rural mail delivery. He was good enough to say that the time was rapidly approaching; I believe he said that before another year was over the department would take up once more the policy of extending the rural mail routes. I, like a good many other members, indeed, I presume like all members of the House, have received from time to time, under the frank of the Postmaster General, copies of the Ottawa Citizen in which reports of conferences and reports of the position of the Post Office department have appeared periodically. I notice in the ministerial press that the Postmaster General, at all events prior to the time of his departure for the south-I do not know what his attitude is just at present-has been pluming himself upon the great success that has attended his efforts in managing the department, especially with respect to its revenues. I understand that last year the Post Office Department showed a surplus. I, of course, have my opinion as to how that surplus was arrived at. When I am at home, I lick a good many stamps for cheques and other things, and I generally use postage stamps. At the same time all that sort of thing goes to swell the revenue of the Post Office Department. In view of what was said last year, I think the time has arrived when the finances of the country will permit, of ihe extension of the rural mail service in Canada. I said last year, and I say now that that is' practically the only direct benefit that many people living in rural communities in this country receive. If they can get a rural mail service, this is of great benefit, in fact, of almost inestimable benefit to them. I can contrast conditions that exist to-day in my province with what they were twenty-five years ago. When I was a boy, we lived in a country district and I had to walk three times a week six miles to get my father's mail. Today there is a daily rural service established by the late government in that particular community, and I say that all communities in the country have a right to look forward to the immediate future when there will be a rural route on every great road, at all events, in this country. I hope, however, there will be no patronage in the extension of that service.
It is by contract.

It is let by contract, and I am not altogether in favour of that system, because my experience is that people in rural communities frequently vie with each other, and the government is getting the service, in many instances, at below cost. I can quote

Supply-Post Office
case after case of this character. I know of a case of a contractor taking a contract immediately before the war who, in the course of the four years his contract ran, went behind one thousand dollars. I know that is a fact, because I had to help him out and I was glad to do so. It was only after the most strenuous efforts that we were able to get that man any increase at all. A contract system in theory is probably quite all right; but in practice it works out that the government gets the service performed by rural mail carriers in this country in many cases at below cost. The time has arrived when the government ought to have a policy and to say that they are going to extend this service to people in rural communities.

difficult to get people in the country to do this work. I mention this as one of the many difficulties which we find prevailing in the rural districts to-day.
Many of the things which the farmers are producing they have to market in competition with the whole world, and the climatic conditions of this country are such as to render that competition all the more difficult. In tropical countries produce can be got out of the land with comparatively no difficulty, and when we in Canada have to compete against such conditions it will easily be seen what a handicap we are under. I might mention several articles produced under such favourable conditions that come into this country to the value of millions of dollars. For instance, we hear a great deal of talk about wool, the raw material of the manufactured product, upon which a high tariff is maintained, coming in free of competition. This is the system that prevails, and so long as it does prevail it seems that contracts must be let by tender for the rural mail service. But I cannot see any justification for paying the letter carrier in the city the salary he gets today, together with his uniform-I believe he gets two suits-and giving the rural man the remuneration which he now receives. I should like the minister to justify the difference in these two cases. He might also tell us what is the average amount paid to the rural letter carrier on a twenty or twenty-five mile route and also the average salary paid to the letter carrier in the city. At the same time I would ask whether there have been so far many losses in connection with the dividends paid on war loans which are distributed in the rural districts. The cheques are sent out in an ordinary brown envelope very similar to the envelopes that contain the applications in connection with the Civil Service Commission, and I have often thought that the envelopes containing these cheques should be registered instead of being sent out in the indiscriminate way in which they are delivered at present. Very often they are put into the wrong box, because unfortunately many of the carriers are not very careful; and in many cases there is no choice in the selection of these men on account of the competitive system. So far, have there been many losses in this respect? I know myself of some that have occurred in connection with cheques issued in payment of interest on war loan bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not tell my hon. friend offhand, but I do not think there have been extensive losses. There may be an exceptional case here and there, but there have been no widespread losses.

Would it involve any difficulty in having these cheques registered? I do not think it would entail any extra cost to the government, and it would make for safety. At all events it would be much more satisfactory than having the cheques distributed in the indiscriminate way in which they are sent out at present. Very often children are sent to the boxes to get mail during stormy weather and it is quite possible that an important bit of mail might be blown away. There is another matter which I would bring to the attention of the minister, and that is with regard to legal holidays on which the rural mail carriers have to deliver mail. Surely it is only fair that they should be given some remuneration for delivering mail on legal holidays. They have to carry the mails in all kinds of weather and they get nothing for their services on these holidays. I think it is only fair that they should be given something for this extra work.

The last point raised by my hon. friend is worth consideration, and perhaps an amount might be added to provide remuneration for work clone on holidays. Perhaps something might be provided to enable a man to engage someone else to drive his mail on that day if necessary. But it must be borne in mind that these men know all the terms and conditions when they take the contract. However, it is worth considering whether it would not be just to do something in this regard, as my hon. friend suggests. As to the delivery of war loan cheques, my experience is that one of the reasons why business men use cheques is because they do not have to register them. The cheque is usually payable to order and if it is lost payment can be stopped. We have not heard many complaints in the Post Office Department as to the loss of cheques. Personally I seldom get a cheque, although I send out cheques often enough. Whenever I do so, however, I always make the cheque payable' to order and never register it.

I want to put a further question regarding some information that was attempted to be elicited by hon. members from Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) and Victoria, (Alta.) (Mr. Lucas). Does the minister seriously mean that there is no contract of any kind with the railway companies that carry our mail? We have been informed that they do not go out and grab for the nearest mail sack, and we can readily accept this information. We have been further informed that the onus rests on the postal employees. Is there any arrangement made

Supply-Post Office
between the Post Office Department and the railway companies so that the latter know about what amount of mail, when, and between what points they are to carry it? On the other hand, does the Post Office Department know what trains are going to carry mail on certain dates? Surely there must be some arrangement under which the Post Office Department and the railway companies know how the mails are to be handled.
There is no agreement with the railway companies as to the mails they shall carry.
Not as to the amount?

No, as to the mails they shall carry. There is an agreement as to what they shall get for their services, but they are not guaranteed any particular mail. The Post Office Department in its re-arrangement knows generally what railways are carrying certain mails, but the agreement with the railway companies, as I read it to-night, is that they shall get certain payment for the mails they carry. As for the Post Office Department, it can divert the mails in any way; there is no absolute contract with the railway companies that they shall have an absolute mail route.
Is it the intention of the government to appoint very soon a Deputy Minister for the Post Office Department?

The minister himself
would have to be consulted on that matter; as Acting Postmaster General I should not like to give an opinion as to what his views may be. There is an Acting Deputy Postmaster General, and there will probably not be any thought of appointing a deputy permanently until the Postmaster General's return.

My excuse for asking is that I have put the question many times to the Postmaster General himself. While I am on the subject I would suggest that when the government deals with the appointment of the Deputy Postmaster General it give some thought to the present condition in the various departments in Ottawa as to the respective representation of English-speaking and French-speaking deputy ministers. It is a fact that under the old government-I suppose we could not expect anything else from it-the ratio of French-speaking deputy ministers went down practically to nothing. The condition to-day is that there is a Clerk of the Privy Council, Mr. Boudreau, who has the rating of a deputy minister-
Before the hon. gentleman proceeds further, will he tell me what reduction was made by the old government of French-speaking deputy ministers?
I have not got the facts before me.
I have the facts before me. It was one in ten years. As I understand, this government has made a similar reduction in one year.
I know that the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue has disappeared.

For the simple reason that the department was amalgamated with the Customs. That is the only reduction in ten years, but under this government one French-speaking deputy minister has been retired in one year. So why is the hon. gentleman making that statement as to the old government?
I have not the least hesitation to present my case in another way, because the sooner we forget the old government the better.
It is better to forget it than to say the wrong thing about it,

I might put it this way, that during the ten years of the old regime our representation-because I speak for my compatriots-in the different departments as regards deputy ministers was below the standard I am now asking the new government-which is working very hard to right many of the wrongs of its predecessors-when it appoints a Deputy Postmaster General to give thought to the fact that at present the French-speaking people of this country are only represented in the departments by way of deputy ministers by the clerk of the Privy Council, Mr. Boudreau-who has the rank of a deputy minister but without the responsibility of a large department-and by Mr. Des-barats in the Department of National Defence -who is not a deputy minister, I understand, but who since his transfer to that department still retains the salary of a deputy minister. I do not wish to argue the point at length for it speaks for itself. I do not wish even to cast any aspersion on the past; I say again that the sooner we forget the past the better. But when the government of to-day appoints a Deputy Postmaster General I wish it would remember that there are in this country over two and a half million French Canadians who pay their taxes and who should certainly be allowed their proportion of representation in
Supply-Post Office

the departments as anywhere else. That is my proposal.
Would the hon. member be satisfied to have appointed as deputy minister of the department a good Canadian?

I certainly would be
satisfied in a general way; but I think there are good Canadians among the French Canadians; that is my point; and having a bilingual situation we must deal with it as it is. I believe you can find very good Canadians among the French Canadian employees of the Post Office Department. I will not mention any names, although I have brought some names to the attention of the government already. I am perfectly willing to admit the principle that we must have a good Canadian as Deputy Postmaster General, but I wish to protest against any condition where it seems that there are no good Canadians except among the other branch of our people. I strongly urge the government, I would not say exactly to appoint a French Canadian as Deputy Postmaster General, but in a more general and broad way to give the Frenchspeaking people of this country their due representation in that grade of office.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister speaks I would like to say a few words anent the remarks of the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret). Towards the close he became very anxious to forget the subject that he emphasized so pointedly in the first half of his remarks, and begged us all to disregard it. He started to attack the late government and claimed that we had done an injustice to French Canadians in that we had reduced, as he said, almost to the vanishing point the number of French Canadian deputy ministers. He added that the present government was struggling hard to repair the errors of the old government, and he begged them in this particular case to do something to that end. I sought to call his attention to the fact that there was no reduction of French-speaking deputy ministers at all by the late government save in the case of one, and there also we made a reduction of one of the English-speaking deputy ministers, if not two. But the only reason that Mr. Vincent, who was a very competent deputy minister of the Inland Revenue department, was not continued was that the government amalgamated the office with that of the Customs, and very rightly so. I know the hon. member would not say that that was not the proper thing to do. Not only was that the only case, but Mr. Vincent was treated with absolute fairness by

the government, as he himself would admit; I do not think any retiring deputy was ever treated more liberally. Now, the hon. member says that this government is struggling to repair those errors. All this government has done to repair them is to reduce three deputy ministers to two. There were three of French origin when we left office; there are two to-day. Is that not right? There was Sir Eugene Fiset, Deputy Minister of Militia; there was Mr. Desbarats, Deputy Minister of Naval Service; and Mr. Boudreau; there are now only the latter two. So that in the great struggle to repair the errors of the old government, described in such heroic language by my hon. friend, the result has been to diminish-and, as he would view it, to aggravate-the offence of the old government. I know that Bir Eugene Fiset is out not by way of any injustice to him at all-I presume at his own desire; I do not know-but in the amalgamation of the Department of Militia and the Department of Naval Service. All I object to is the continual effort of the hon. member, which, I am sorry to say, he has been guilty of for years, through the paper he edits in Montreal as well as on the floor of this House, to impute to the late government an animosity that never inspired it and that never was in evidence. That was purely a matter of political incitation at the hands of hon. members who sought political advantage by it. I join with the hon. member in the hope that he expresses: I hope that it will be possible to find a French-speaking deputy-minister for the Post Office Department. I know the principal need is to have an efficient man; the hon. member will agree that that should be paramount. But while we are a bilingual country, talk as we will, we cannot get away from the necessity, if we are to have content and good feeling throughout the Dominion, of dividing these important appointments in approximate proportion to the respective populations. We tried to follow that out; we succeeded in almost every respect. I know the contingencies were such that when we went out of office the French Canadians were not getting their fair share in respect to the deputy ministerships. It has to be the practice; no one has more frankly said so year in and year out than myself. Therefore I hope it will be possible in the Post Office Department that a discrepancy that was occasioned in small degree through ten years and in equal degree under this government in one year will be in some respects remedied. The hon. member speaks the whole truth when he says that he has made a recommendation. It is pretty well known through-

Supply-Post Office
out this Dominion that he made a recommendation and that he got a rather curt refusal from the minister.
Oh, no.
It was not curt? It was a refusal, anyway, and it has not been accepted as entirely satisfactory by the friends of my hon. friend.
The matter is pending.

Well, it was pending in
an unfortunate and rather harrowing way when that letter was written. Does the hon. member think there is still hope after that letter?

Well, I hope my hon.
friend's remarks will not do away with that hope.

I hope not too. In fact, I will go further. I have an acquaintance with the gentleman the hon. member recommends. I not only have his personal acquaintance- not in any great degree, because he never was of my political faith; in fact, so far as I know he never was a political friend-but I have heard of him for many years and of his services in the department. For myself I know of no reason why he would not make an excellent deputy minister. I hope that will help my hon. friend.
It might.

If it does, I shall be very much pleased. I earnestly hope that the trouble that has arisen over the matter will be patched up and that there will be no serious or permanent schism as a result. I rose only to state what I believed to be the principle that ought to be adopted and to express the earnest hope that something can be done to live up to it in the appointment of a deputy minister of this department.

We are not on the civil government estimates, under which I suppose, the matter of the deputy minister might be dealt with. But as the item will probably go through without much discussion when we come to it, perhaps it is just as well that we should deal with it now. I may say that I know of no decision having been arrived at in the matter of the deputy ministership; none has been conveyed to me. My right hon. friend stated a truism in a three-cornered fashion when he intimated that this government had reduced the number of Frenchspeaking deputies. But the fact is that this government did not do that. Sir Eugene Fiset, against my protest until his doctor's certificate was handed to me, insisted upon
resigning. If at the end of his term of leave of absence his health should be sufficiently recovered to enable him to resume his work, nothing would delight me more, because he is one of the ablest deputies there ever was in this country.
If he had not resigned, Mr. Desbarats could not be deputy of the department; so there would have been a reduction anyway.
I am not so sure about that.
How could you have one department and two deputies?
It was so in the Marine and Fisheries department; there was a Deputy Minister of Naval Defence and a Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

But the minister has
made Naval Service and Militia one department. How can he have two deputies in one department?

Under one ministerial
head.
No, there were two departments.
I beg my right hon. friend's pardon.
I know it, and the minister knows it too.

May I say a word? The bill I introduced in this House forming the amalgamation provided for two deputies. The Upper Chamber amended the bill so that that was impossible, but it was provided that Mr. Desbarats should be retained in the new department as controller of the finances with the salary of a deputy minister. When Sir Eugene Fiset insisted on obtaining leave of absence, which I reluctantly gave him on account of his great ability and long experience, Mr. Desbarats remained Deputy Minister of Naval Service and assumed the office of Acting Deputy Minister of the Department of Defence. He is now controller and acting deputy. He cannot be appointed deputy, because two men cannot draw salaries for the same position. Sir Eugene Fiset is still drawing salary. When his leave of absence expires, if he is not able to return to his work, it will be in order to appoint a new deputy. I simply wanted to make it clear that the government was reluctant to part with Sir Eugene Fiset and that it was at his own request he was given leave of absence. Now, I will direct the attention of the Postmaster Gen-

eral to the discussion which has taken place here to-night. I have a great deal of sympathy with the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Rinfret). In this country, where we have a bilingual situation, we who are in the majority must see to it that those in the minority have fair play in respect to these larger positions, because only by showing that spirit can we hope to have unity and amity throughout the country.

I do not wish to prolong this debate, but I would like to say this. I did not withdraw at all, as the right hon. leader of the Opposition suggests, from the position I first took, but as that was not my point I simply did not wish to stress it. I could mention very easily many cases both in the service and elsewhere where we claim we did not get justice from the late government, and I would not like the leader of the Opposition to-day to state that after making a mild statement at first, I was quite willing to withdraw. My only idea in not stressing the point was that it had little to do with the case I was presenting to the committee tonight.
The leader of the Opposition claims that when Mr. Vincent was withdrawn, he was well treated. I do not discuss that phase of the question. I will say, though, that when we claim a certain proportion of responsibility for Ffench-Canadians in the service we are not thinking at all of any huge salary that may happen to be paid to one of them, but we are thinking of the responsibility for those under him, and even if Mr. Vincent was well provided for and I suppose he was, at the same time it meant a loss of responsibility and power for the element he was supposed to represent.
As for the present government, my right hon. friend himself will admit that it has only been in power a year and a half, so we cannot very well consider that it has yet had the opportunity to do all that it wanted to do. The reason why I am asking this government to give proportional representation in that sense is that I feel perfectly satisfied that it will in due time, and I am taking the first occasion that offers itself to bring the attention of the government to that point.
There is just another remark I would like to make before I sit down. My right hon. friend has said that in my paper, referring to Le Canada of Montreal, and in my speeches I never lose an opportunity or I often take occasion to raise prejudice and create bad feeling. That was his statement, if I am not mistaken. I am not prepared at all to admit that. I am expressing the views of a certain proportion of the population who do not share

the views of my right hon. friend, but I always try to do it in a very moderate way and in a spirit of good understanding. I am ready to admit, however, that neither my paper nor any of my speeches are intended to please the leader of the Opposition.

I have sent for the statutes because I am afraid the statutes will be necessary to convince the minister that there were two departments. There was a Naval Service department and a Marine and Fisheries department. They were created at different times. They were not one department.
They were under one minister.

Certainly. Very frequently a minister has two departments. The Minister of the Interior has three to-day. The Minister of Interior is Minister of Mines; he is Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs, that is another department; he is Minister of the Interior. He is head of three departments with three deputy ministers. But the Minister of Militia made the Department of Militia and Defence and the Department of Naval Service, not two departments under one minister, but one department.
It was intended to make them one department with two deputy heads.

That was the anomaly of the whole thing. You cannot have two deputy heads. The minister tried to do that and he was very readily cured. It was only a method of keeping the salary that was all. That was what the minister was after. What the minister objected to in my remarks and in which I was absolutely right is this. I said there were two departments not one. The
11 p.m. Marine and Fisheries department was one and the Naval Service department was wholly different. I have before me the statutes now which I can read to the minister. The Naval Service was created by Chapter 43 9-10 Edward VII, and the first thing the act says is that there shall be a Department of Naval Service. There had been a Department of Marine and Fisheries years before that. It was created by chapter 45 of the statutes of 1906. No, that is the chapter marked by the Library staff, but it is not the one I sent for. The Marine and Fisheries department was created very many years ago, shortly after confederation. There were two departments under one minister, and there were two deputy ministers. The Minister of the Interior has now three deputy ministers, and quite properly, in fact four, for Immigration has been put under him. There are

Supply-Post Office
four different departments. That is a wholly * different thing. But when the Minister of Militia took the responsibility of combining the Naval Service with Militia and Defence by that act he necessarily got rid not of a deputy minister from the service but of the office and salary of a deputy minister, because you can have only one deputy to a department. He did precisely the same as we had done with the Department of Customs and Inland Revenue. That is all I rose to say. I do not say he should not have done it; I do not say that at all, but when one complains of the result of our action in ten years I would point out that the same thing has resulted under this government in one year.
I have nothing further to say in answer to the hon. member (Mr. Rinfret). He was pretty fair in his reply. I certainly cannot dispute his initial statement that he could tell me of many cases where he claimed to be unjustly treated. I know he was continually claiming that almost every day for ten years.

I do not know what particular item we are discussing, but I think this is perhaps an appropriate time to bring to the attention of the minister a suggestion which appears to me might have some merit in it. Under the law as it stands at present, public libraries I believe are entitled to a special postage rate on books sent out within a radius of fifty miles. That is a very desirable provision. The only point I wish to question is the limitation as to mileage. In eastern Canada I can quite understand that that limitation is very effective and perhaps meets the situation, but in western Canada with our great distances it is not, I think, working as satisfactorily. For instance, we have a public library at Edmonton and another at the city of Calgary, 190 miles away. The result is that with a fifty-mile zone, the libraries are not able to secure the advantage of the lessened postage rates, and consequently the reading public who might otherwise secure the advantage of books from public libraries are not able to secure them owing to the postage rates. My hon. friend from Edmonton reminds me that this is a very serious matter in the northern part of the province. The closest library is Edmonton, and the country to be served extends some three or four hundred miles north from that point. I rose simply for the purpose of suggesting to the minister that the zone be increased perhaps to one hundred miles. In that way no harm would be done in eastern Canada, but it would advantage the West very considerably.

I would like to refer back to a question that has been before the House already to-night. One or two members have made the statement that they have not been approached with regard to the appointments of postmasters where the salary has been under $200. I jokingly remarked that I had not been consulted in the matter, but perhaps I did not give the House a correct impression. I want to say that I have no desire to be consulted in the matter. I just wished to correct a mistaken impression some hon. members may have got from my remark. I would like to deal with that just for a moment. It would seem that the department is asking certain members of this House to make recommendations of the names of persons who, they think, would be capable of occupying these positions. Who is responsible for that? Who is going to be responsible for the appointment of that official in a position with a salary of $200? Does the department hold the member of parliament responsible for his recommendation? Or is the department going to hold itself responsible for that appointment? I maintain that, if they are asking the members of the House of Commons to recommend the names of people for those positions, the system is wrong, and we ought to get away from it as soon as we possibly can. I contend that where positions in small post offices become vacant the department should be responsible for seeing that a proper person is appointed to that particular vacancy, and it is not a question of a member of the House recommending any person for that particular vacancy. We must at all times hold the Post Office Department responsible for the appointments, and I hope and trust the department will get away from the species of petty patronage that has been introduced during the last twelve months.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
